utterances.text: I don't think that this list includes names of KLA soldiers. We did not consider KLA soldiers as civilian victims. So us they were heroes, people's heroes, because they took up weapons to defend the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I take it from your response that you supported the KLA during the war. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Not only me, but the entire Albanian population in Kosova supported the KLA. I'm just one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, now I'd like to ask you about what you testified here earlier. You mentioned a second list with KLA members, and that is the list that I'm asking you about. Did you provide a copy of that list to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't remember. I can tell you the number that occurs on that list, but I don't know if I offered that list to the Prosecutor's office or not. I know that I provided the Prosecutor's office with two lists: The first list of civilian victims and the second extended list. If there is a third list, maybe I did offer it to them but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, you mentioned at page 80, line 23 through 25 of today's transcript that there is a list of soldiers and you said it's "another one." So I want to ask you: How many fallen KLA soldiers from the municipality of Suva Reka appear on this second list which you may or may not have given to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to be clear. The list that I offered to the Office of the Prosecutor includes names of civilian victims that were killed in Suhareke municipality. It has nothing to do with the list of soldiers that the counsel is putting to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your earlier evidence you said there were no KLA soldiers on the list. You said it was a list of civilians, and you then said: "The list of soldiers is another one, so they are not on this one." Now, what counsel is asking you is about what you appear to have said was a separate list of soldiers. Now, is there such a list? Well, his questions are directed to that. So bear that in mind when you're trying to answer them. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now this question is clear to me. I said earlier that there is a list of soldiers who were killed on the front line. To my knowledge, this list includes the names of 83 martyrs but this list was not presented to the ICTY investigators in my part because I did not deal with -- I was not involved in the investigations of martyrs that were killed. My work dealt strictly dealt with investigation of victims, civilian victims that were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And to ensure that we have the whole picture, were these 83 deceased all within the Suva Reka municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, limiting ourselves to the Suva Reka municipality, is it accurate that during 1998 and 1999 the 123rd Brigade of the so-called KLA was operating in that area and had approximately 1.600 armed fighters in its structure?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: It is true that 123rd Brigade was operating in Suhareke municipality, but I don't know the number of soldiers it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it also accurate that the 123rd Brigade of the KLA controlled various villages and territory within the Suva Reka municipality?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: It was in mountainous and hilly regions. The population that was forced to withdraw for security reasons, that area was under the protection of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it -- is my understanding correct from your response that you have knowledge of the fact that the KLA ordered the Albanian civilian population to move at various times in the Suva Reka municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Objection. I don't believe the witness has any basis for answering that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the answer is such that I would have asked the question if Mr. Ivetic hadn't asked it. The answer that was given was: "They were in control in the mountainous and hilly areas where the population had to withdraw for security reasons." I see nothing wrong with the question that's been asked to follow that up. Carry on with it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'll ask the question again. Is my understanding correct from your response that you have knowledge of the fact that the KLA ordered the ethnic Albanian civilian population to move at various times from various villages in the Suva Reka municipality?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No. The Kosovo Liberation Army never directed or ordered the civilian population to leave their own villages. The civilian population sought shelter after the attacks that were undertaken by the Serbian -- Yugoslav army and police by shelling villages from different directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the -- during the time-period of January through March 1999, did you ever have contact with any officers of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Could you state the time-period again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. The time-period I stated was January 1999 through March 1999.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, I have never contacted any officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then -- well, I see that the time period -- well, how about in 1998 or ...

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The Kosovo Liberation Army did not operate in the city of Suhareke. It was never present, neither in 1998 nor in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But it did exist and operate in a majority of the villages that surrounded and were adjacent to Suva Reka town. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I'm speaking about Suhareke because I was always there, in Suhareke, and I can speak about the army and police forces, the Yugoslav army and police forces that I came across during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Now, you stated in your direct examination that the Territorial Defence was under the authority and control of the police forces. Are you aware of the -- of the laws of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia that were in existence during the time-period of 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I know that there were laws about killing as many Albanians as possible, and that's what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, as a lawyer, could you please cite to me a law that called for the killing of as many Albanians as possible, or are you perhaps giving false testimony?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: First of all, I have to remind you, sir, and the accused here, that in March 1999 before the NATO bombing started, you threatened the Albanian population with the words that: If NATO bombs the Serbian forces and positions, we will expel the Albanians. On the 24th of March, in the afternoon, in addition to the reinforcements that were coming to Kosova all the time, police forces and army forces were coming from Serbia at that time and they were stationed in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm still waiting for you to answer my question to cite the specific law that you referenced that said that all Albanians should be killed, or was that perhaps false testimony on your part?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No. This is not false testimony, but I'm speaking about the facts that we've lived --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would ask you to cite the law.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: There were orders outside the law. You proclaimed a state of war in Kosova and you gave all the rights to the Yugoslav army and police to act as aggressively and cruelly as possible against the Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that you have neither examined nor made inquiry about the laws that were in effect on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia and the autonomous province of Kosovo-Metohija during 1998/1999 that would enable you to draw the conclusions that you've reached regarding the Territorial Defence being under the control of the MUP or the existence of any laws to "kill as many Albanians as possible"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Objection, asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe I've been trying to get an answer for some time, but I don't believe it's been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Direct me, please, Mr. Scully to the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the best answer is: There were orders outside the law. And while that's not in the terms that counsel's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no, that was the different -- well, yeah. The problem with that question, Mr. Ivetic, is you've combined the two issues. You've combined the emotive one, which I think we've probably moved past, with the question you started this with, which was whether there was any law which placed the Territorial Defence under the control of the MUP. And that's what I think this question should be confined to. And if it is, I don't think Mr. Scully can object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. That's what I meant to confine it. Perhaps I got carried away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's be absolutely clear by asking the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it a fact that you have neither examined nor made inquiry into the laws that were in effect on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Republic of Serbia, and/or the autonomous province of Kosovo-Metohija in 1998 and 1999 that would enable you to draw any conclusions about the operations of either the Territorial Defence or the MUP, and in particular the subordination of the Territorial Defence to the MUP as you testified to in your direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's exactly the same question. He's testified that he did examine the law and that what he's referring to is the orders -- I've lost the term now, but the orders outside the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the question doesn't help, Mr. Ivetic. I thought that there was a particular point here that you were trying to undermine, which was the basis for saying that the police had authority over the Territorial Defence. But your question's a much more general one which --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I could ask it specifically that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- I don't think the witness should be required to deal with again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's ask him this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have a factual legal basis for your conclusion that the police had authority over the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Once again I will have to repeat this. Sir, you're making the question in different forms, but I said earlier, and I'll repeat it again. All the actions undertaken in Kosova against the civilian population were commanded by the head of the Serbian state and the former Yugoslavia. And all the orders were given by that leadership. And they were implemented by the police, the army, in cooperation with each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is there a part in the statement where the particular point relating to the Territorial Defence is made?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, I do not recall, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I assumed that this related to a particular statement within the statement, but it appears it was a more general question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was only new that I thought came up in the direct, so I did not have anything on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think this matter is going to be advanced by any further questions on this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. I'm prepared to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your statement you describe that on the 25th of March in the morning you saw flames of burning houses. Now, you did not actually see the houses as to how they were set on fire, did you?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I would like to describe the whole event before the 25th of March. Before the -- 6.00 in the morning on that day, how the Serbian forces penetrated and they attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, one of the prerogatives of doing a cross-examination is choosing the questions that are asked. We have your statement, we have your testimony, and I'm trying to clarify specific points of it. So I would ask you again: The houses that you say were burning on the morning of the 25th of March from paragraph 3 of your statement, you did not personally see these houses and how they were set ablaze, did you?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The police and the army set those houses on fire; I saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, you're being asked -- well, sorry, you have answered it now by saying that you did see the police and the army setting them ablaze, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You personally saw them. And how did they set the houses on fire, sir?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I saw the police. They had this, special guns that they threw flames with those guns. They had them on their backs and they had the form of beer bottles and that's how they set the houses on fire. I don't know what was inside those bottles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, how do you explain the fact that in one statement that you gave consisting of ten pages, a supplemental statement that you gave consisting of one page, and testimony before the Milosevic Trial Chamber, you never once testified that you saw these houses being set ablaze. Why is it you have now changed your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Objection to the characterisation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what's wrong with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: He hasn't changed his testimony; he's simply added information to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic, that seems to be strictly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you explain for us why you have added to your prior testimony? Why did you not testify to this previously if in fact you saw it with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I'm not adding anything. You're saying why I did not say this. When I spoke in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic, time was limited and I was not allowed to explain everything in detail. So if you ask the question now, I'm completed -- I'm completing what I said in Milosevic's trial; that's what I'm doing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How far were you from the burning houses, those that we are talking about now, the ones that you saw on the 25th of March in the morning?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, these were a little further away. My brothers were there in that area, about 600 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What time of day did you see them being set ablaze or night, if it was night?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: It was not important to know. There was so many gun-shots around. It was an offensive of the army and the police together. They were walking and shooting and burning and shelling, killing people. There were lots of gun-shots and the flames, you could see the flames.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, I'm afraid I'm now confused. On what date do you say that you saw police using flame-throwers to set houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both on the 25th, 26th, 28th, 27th as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, when you were asked: How far were you from the burning houses on the 25th, you said that they were about 600 metres away and it was your brothers that were in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you saying you observed this from 600 metres away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The smoke and the flames could be seen even farther away, not the 600 metres that I mentioned. Even the gun-shots --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that entirely. It's the identification of who's actually setting fire to the houses that's an issue. And a moment ago I got the impression you actually saw people using flame-throwers to set houses on fire. I'm now getting the impression you didn't actually see it with your own eyes, and it's important we're clear about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I described the event not only of the 25th, but also 26th, 27th, 28th, the 3rd of April, and so on. If we focus only on the 25th, as I said, on the 25th I was 600 metres away as the crow flies and it was 6.00 in the morning. I saw the smoke and the flames and I heard the gun-shots. I did not say that I was very close and I saw them. The families who were there in the area saw what happened, and among those families were my brothers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On what date did you personally see anyone actually set fire to a house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 3rd of April of 1999, when the police forces, the Serb police forces, came to the place where I was sheltered with my wife and my five children. They came shooting in our direction, where I was. And they were setting the houses on fire. That's where I saw directly and with my own eyes that they had these flame-throwers on their backs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic. Oh, sorry, is this a suitable time to interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, Mr. Berisha, we have a half-hour break at this stage, so please leave the courtroom and return at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I've got approximately two areas I want to ask you questions about now, and then I will be completed. Now, you talk about the time period when you left Suva Reka and in my version it's the eighth paragraph of your statement, your written statement, you talk about how the column you were in or the convoy you were in was stopped by a Milan Sipka. And you claim that he ordered the whole column to return back to their homes. Now, do you know what position Mr. Sipka had at that time within the structure of the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know whether I should explain how we were forced to leave our homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think -- confine the answer to the question you've been asked. What position did Mr. Sipka hold in the structure of the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that before 1998, that is before the war, Milan Sipka was commander of the police station in Suhareke. From there he was transferred to Prizren. I don't know what position he held there; I have no information. And I know this as well, that he was from Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, would it be accurate to state that the SUP in Prizren was a much larger police organ than the OUP in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Suhareke was under the jurisdiction of the Prizren region.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So when you say he was transferred to Prizren, would you regard that as being a promotion of Mr. Sipka?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Of course the accused here behind you must know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, did you see -- on the occasion that you had to deal with Mr. Sipka when he told the convoy to return to its homes, did he have on any type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did that police uniform have any rank insignia?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I can't remember the rank insignia because it was getting darker, but I know that it was dark blue camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to direct your attention when you did in fact return to Suva Reka. You talk about an incident at page 5 of your statement, the last paragraph, an incident that occurred on the 21st of May where you identify people who ordered you to leave the house as being Sinisa Andrejevic, who was a local paramilitary from Suva Reka, Nikica Petkovic, brother of Zoran, and another person with the last name Milisav Gogic who were with the DB under Misko Nisevic. There was also another guy by the name of Ramiz who was with the regular police. Now, I want to ask you about this person, Mr. Nisevic, did he wear a uniform on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I did not meet Nisevic that day. The inspector of the state security, while with regard to the group of policemen who came from door to door, from house to house, and ordered the civilian population to leave their houses in ten minutes and get to the main road and go to Albania. This was a strict order. The whole population had to leave and go to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You stated that the gentleman came in a red Golf motor vehicle. Am I correct that the red Golf motor vehicle did not have any insignia of the police on it?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: It -- you are talking about Sinisa Andrejevic, who was a policeman in Suhareke, and all the other ones were policemen as well. They were in a civilian vehicle, and why they were in a civilian vehicle, it's -- I don't know. I identified those people as policemen because they were wearing police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you know this Ramiz person prior to this incident?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, I knew them before, before that day, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in fact, Ramiz is an ethnic Muslim and not a Serb. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: But not Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe I said he was. Now, the last question I have for you is essentially: Is it accurate that after this event you were asked by Andrejevic why you had not gone to help cover trenches that had been dug by the KLA. And I want to ask you: Where were these KLA trenches located that you had been ordered or asked to fill in? Were they in Suva Reka town or were they in the villages?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, they were not in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm finished with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, we have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac -- Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise, Your Honour, we don't have any questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Scully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, drawing your attention to the questions in cross-examination about the temporary government in Kosovo. Did that temporary government tell you what to investigate?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, it didn't. The government didn't tell me what to do. I explained earlier that we had to identify all the people who were missing, and we had family members of those people who were missing wanted to find where they were, people from Suhareke and the surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Thank you. In deciding to put a person on your list of missing and killed, what information did you review?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: In the beginning when the infantry of the -- of NATO troops entered Kosova and then also they entered Suhareke, and because I was all the time there, I did not leave Suhareke, with the exception of the period from the 23rd of May to the 12th of June. So when the NATO forces entered, we knew as family members what tragedy had happened to our family. So I first went and looked at the houses for any traces of the crimes, and then I went and looked at the grave sites. Some of them had a plank with initials of the victims. Then there were others that had the code NN, and because the family members started to dig up these grave sites to find their loved ones - and I feared that the traces of the crimes would be lost - I contacted the Tribunal's office in Prizren and asked for their help, for them to help us to dig up those grave sites and help us identify the missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Did you also talk to living family members about whether they had seen the missing people?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. When the family members returned from Albania, we kept constant contact with them and I got information from them. From June 1999 to this day, I still keep in contact with family members. And I'm working for the investigation of the cases of the people who are missing, because even today in the municipality of Suhareke there are over 160 people still missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Drawing your attention now to the period of January to May of 1999, did you ever see a member of the KLA active in the town of Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, never. The KLA was not present then and it was never present in the city of -- in the town of Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Final couple questions, Mr. Berisha. During cross-examination you described a red Golf that carried regular police officers. Did you ever see any other civilian vehicles used by regular police officers in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They used those vehicles, but they also robbed the vehicles of the Albanian population. I don't know where -- when exactly this was, but it was either on the 8th or the 9th of April when we were told to return, and we returned. And Ismet Hoxha's vehicle was parked in my courtyard -- my brother's courtyard, and these policemen who were in the red Golf, they took the car. And I was there, I saw it. And there were many other cases when they looted the vehicles and they even told the people to get off the cars and took their cars away. On the 4th of April, when we were in the convoy in the village of Korisha, my cousin, Ismet Berisha, his vehicle was taken. His mother who was 90 years old was forced to get off the car, and then they took the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions, other than to move to admit the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Berisha, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give it and to add to the information you had given before. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next Prosecution witness is Mrs. Aferdita Hajrizi, and I'm going to change places with Mr. Scully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is also 92 bis (D)?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this is a 92 bis (D) witness. She testifies about events in the municipality of Mitrovica, and the paragraphs relevant to her testimony are 72(f), 73, 76, and 77 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Hajrizi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can stand up. The microphone will catch you. Would you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Hajrizi, could you please state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I am Aferdita Hajrizi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Hajrizi, in 1999 were you living in the town of Mitrovica in Mitrovica municipality?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecution on 3rd June 1999 and later amended that statement on 31 January of 2002?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: There were only some corrections that I made with reference to the translation, no other corrections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Did you provide a second statement dated 20th August, 2001, which you also later made small corrections on 6th March 2002?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Again, corrections in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in 2002, in April 2002, did you testify before this Tribunal in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honours, I would like to tender this witness's 92 bis evidence under the current Rule 92 ter. The different statements have been assigned different exhibit numbers, so these are P2319, P2320 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You need to tell me which is which. 2319 is which?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is the first statement dated June 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: P2320 is the second statement with its addendum of 6th March, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: P2321 is the transcript of her previous testimony in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And there's also an exhibit attached to that transcript which is P51, which is a file from the Mitrovica court relating to the events that this witness describes in her evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the corrections on the 6th of March, 2002?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: These are together with the second statement of 20th August, so this is Exhibit 2320.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the corrections on the 31st of January, 2002?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 2319. The statements have been put together with their respective amendments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Hajrizi, your written -- your statements and your prior testimony are before this Court. I'm going to ask you some very specific questions on your evidence, and I would like you, if possible, to give me short answers so we can proceed efficiently today. In your statement of 3 -- 3rd June, 1999, you describe how your husband Agim Hajrizi and two members of your family were murdered in your home on the night between 24th and 25th March, 1999. I understand from your statement that your late husband was at the time the chairman of a trade union association, a local trade union association in Mitrovica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was this association working to defend the rights of Albanian workers in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And would it be correct to say that your husband, Mr. Agim Hajrizi?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Agim --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry for mispronouncing the name. Agim Hajrizi was quite a prominent figure in the Albanian community in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other activists being murdered around the same date as the murder of your husband -- in -- I'm speaking about the town of Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes -- [In English] May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the very same night, that is the night between 24th and 25th of March, 1999, another activist was killed, the chairman of the LDK for Mitrovica municipality, Latif Berisha, on the same night when my husband, my son, and my mother-in-law were killed. It was just an hour, I would say, between the two killings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when did you find out about the killing of Latif Berisha?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I found out about the killing of Latif Berisha in the morning of 25th of March when the local radio in Kosova broadcast the news that two prominent activists from Mitrovica were killed, namely Latif Berisha, chairman of the LDK in Mitrovica; and Agim Hajrizi, chairman of the Independent Kosova Trade Union Assembly and his 60-years-old mother, Nazmija and his 11 and a half-year-old son Ilir. This is the news that was broadcast on local radios and I heard it in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did both of these killings occur shortly after the beginning of the NATO bombings in the area?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I have also stated this in my previous statements that as you may know the night of the 24th of March, 1999, was the night when the NATO forces began their bombing campaign against the Serb aggression that was exercised on the Albanian population, and all this pressure on the Albanian population intensified from that night on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Hajrizi, I'm --

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: The pressure exercised on the Albanian population took years. It was old, not from that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to focus specifically on your first statement, the one on 3rd June. You describe in quite some detail the murders of your family members, and I don't want to go into all that detail here. But on page 6 of your statement you say that you saw six men arrive to your house dressed in blue camouflage uniforms and wearing black berets on the night of 24 March. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise any of these men?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who were you able to recognise among these six men?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I stated with full responsibility in my statement - and I will repeat it today - that on that night there were two vehicles parked in front of my house, they are of dark colour. The two drivers were inside these vehicles, and six persons, Serb paramilitary police members, were in my courtyard. I could recognise two of them Nenad Pavicevic who was my first neighbour, and his friend Dejan [as interpreted]. I didn't know his last name. And two others, Dejan Savic and Ratko Antonijevic were identified by my husband. And the fifth and the sixth, we did not recognise them. We did not know them, neither me nor my husband. The last two names, Ratko and Dejan, have stuck in my mind because my husband's last words were, and I quote: "If anything happens to me, because you know that they are not this by accident, wearing uniforms and heavily armed, they're here to commit a crime." I remember these words, and that's why I'm stating this with full responsibility before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The two -- of the two that you recognised you've given one of them today the name "Dejan." Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The person that I recognised, his name was Boban, and the other one Nenad, while Dejan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on. It may have been a problem with the translation, but you've now clarified it and we can now move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, there is one other thing before we move on. In the court in Mitrovica, a person accused there was acquitted called Gligorovski. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His name was Lazar Gligorovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in the first statement you gave about this, the one that Ms. Kravetz is asking you about, you referred to a person called Djordjevski. Is that a different person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is why I made the correction. Gligorovski should stand for Djordjevski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Hajrizi, you just referred to these men as Serb paramilitary policemen. What did you mean by that when you said that they were Serb paramilitary policemen that arrived to your house?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: What I meant was the following. I will explain it to you. For decades in the streets of Mitrovica and in the streets throughout Kosova, we were used to seeing military and police uniforms of the day. And what do I mean with the word of "the day"? Meaning while on duty they were wearing another uniform. Your Honours, if you only saw those paramilitary uniforms that we saw at night, if you only saw members of the paramilitary formation Black Hand, their uniforms, their weapons, their knives, terrible knives, you would be able to understand who these paramilitaries were and what was the difference between the uniforms of the ordinary police and the uniforms of the paramilitaries and the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Hajrizi, I'm going to rephrase the question. You said you identified two of these persons, one of them by the name of Nenad Pavicevic. Did you know if this person was a police officer in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the second person you identified, that you were able to recognise that night --

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Both of them, both of them. Nenad Pavicevic and his friend Boban, they both were policemen of the Yugoslav police. They were serving in the Yugoslav police. They had police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Hajrizi --

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: The same is true for the others that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, out of these four persons, are you aware of whether there were any prosecutions later against these persons in connection with the murder of your husband?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: After I returned from Holland in December 1999, two or three months later there was a hearing at which Lazar Gligorovski was being tried who was imprisoned at that time --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for the four persons you mentioned that were --

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In addition to Lazar Gligorovski, Nenad Pavicevic was being tried in absence. They didn't know anything about his whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you testify in those proceedings?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And are you aware of what was the outcome of -- of that trial, if anyone was convicted as a result of that trial?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do know. Nenad Pavicevic was sentenced to 20 years of imprisonment in absentia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, this -- the judgement in this case is before Your Honours as Exhibit P51. It's part of this witness's 92 bis material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Before -- yeah, thank you. Before you move on, though, just going back to the previous issue where we were given a description of paramilitary uniforms, the witness then appeared to say that all of these people were members of the regular police force. What is the evidence that you're seeking to lead on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm understanding from the witness's testimony that these four -- four of the six -- at least the four persons she was able to identify were regular police officers who -- went into her house, but it also appears that she refers to them as being police -- or paramilitary police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: She said that: "Both of them, Pavicevic and his friend Boban were both policemen of the Yugoslav police. They were serving in the Yugoslav police. They had police uniforms. The same is true for the others that I mentioned."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm confused. I don't know who it's being suggested was a paramilitary police officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I can maybe try to clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Hajrizi, you mentioned just a couple of minutes ago that the four persons you were able to recognise were police officers in Mitrovica. Are you stating -- or is it your evidence that these men were also members of a paramilitary group or what you understand to be a paramilitary group, a non-regular armed group?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Again, I'm stating with full responsibility that these two that I recognised were members or employees of the Serbian police. However, considering the fact that maybe ten times during the day I have seen him with regular police uniform, since he was my neighbour, and on the night of the crime I've seen him with a paramilitary uniform, with that dark blue uniform, a horrifying uniform, it clearly shows that even within the ranks of regular police there were infamous paramilitary groups operating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But, Mrs. Hajrizi, we have heard evidence that dark blue camouflage uniforms were worn by the regular police. Are you saying that they were only worn by people you understood to be paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Hajrizi, you have to speak an answer. The transcript is not going to reflect your answer if you don't speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the ordinary police uniform, the uniform of the Yugoslav police consisted of a light blue colour shirt and dark blue trousers. The uniform that was worn by paramilitaries was something different; it was dark blue, camouflage, in dark black patterns, with black berets. And the weapons that the police, the ordinary police of the Yugoslav army carried, was different from the weapons that the paramilitaries carried. I do not recognise all the types of weapons, and I do not want to do that. But you could tell that they were different as for their shape and size.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what you've described earlier was that they were -- I think you referred to carrying knives. Is that ... Are these the different weapons you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The paramilitary police that carried out the massive expulsion of the Albanian population from Kosova carried long weapons with knives at the top, and they carried knives on their belt.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Hajrizi --

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- can I ask a question. Are you aware whether these persons you are describing as paramilitaries worked together with the persons you described as regular policemen? If you don't know, you can state so.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you could repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You have described some men as paramilitaries in dark blue camouflage uniform, and you said the regular police wore solid blue uniform. Are you aware of whether these men that you described as paramilitaries, if they worked together or jointly with the men that you described as regular police. And again, if you don't know, you can say so.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I don't know about others. As for the two that I recognised and identified, yes, I can say they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I should try to help in clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Now, are you trying to -- you know English, please. Are you trying to tell us that some of the people from the police whom you have called as infamous people like Boban they later changed their dress so that they were not -- they were camouflaged or they did not show up themselves and joined this paramilitary group with a black dress for this specific purpose, and not that en masse the police force used to change its dress and become a paramilitary police. It's only a few infamous people in the police who came and joined these type of scare groups. Are you saying this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Hajrizi. I would like to move on. I'm not going to explore that subject further because you address the murders of your family members in quite some detail in your statement, so I'd like to move on to your second statement of 20th August, 2001. On page 3 of that statement you say that in the days following the murders you moved to the neighbourhood of Tavnik [Realtime transcript read in error "Travnik"] in Mitrovica. Can you tell me what was the ethnic composition of the Tavnik neighbourhood in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: It's not Travnik, Tavnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's misspelled, it's Tavnik.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes. The population was mainly Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you moved there, where were you staying for the days following your -- the murders at your house?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: On the morning of the 25th of May, with the help of my brother, I withdrew from the centre of town and went to the suburbs of the town in the neighbourhood Tavnik, where my parents live. At that time my parents were not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. --

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: And I spent some days --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yeah, just finish -- you can finish. I'm sorry. You can finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I spent some days in that neighbourhood, and at the Yugoslav police and army orders, we were forced to leave from the Tavnik neighbourhood --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you were forced to leave the Tavnik neighbourhood. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: We were forced. I repeat, we were forced leave. There were so many killings going on around us. Many houses were set on fire. Many people were taken away and imprisoned. There were so many voices of people that we could hear; that showed us that somebody was forcing these people to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm going to have to interrupt you again. I was asking for the date when this occurred, that you were forced to leave Tavnik neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: This was exactly three days of my husband was killed. It was the 28th of March, 1999, when 70.000 inhabitants of Mitrovica and unprecedented violence exercised by the army and police forces were forced to leave their houses without knowing where they were going. They went towards the direction of Zhabar village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know I've reached the 30-minute time that I have allocated for this witness. I'll just be another five or seven minutes, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That wasn't the order we made. You've used a lot of time muddying waters that were otherwise apparently clear. Is it new material that you seek to embark upon or are you simply going to be asking questions that bring a repetition of what's in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The questions I was going to put are covered by the statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's no need for you to extend your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I have no further questions then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will proceed in the following order: General Lukic, General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Milutinovic, General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Hajrizi. My name is Branko Lukic, and I will have only a few questions for you. In your first statement you talk about August 1998 when someone shouted at you from across the street asking you what were you still doing in Kosovska Mitrovica, after which that person fired a shot at your house, hitting it. That person was subsequently arrested. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your lady neighbour told you that they only asked him why he had used his rifle unless he was ready to carry out his duty. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I did not understand the question. Could you repeat that, please. I don't think it was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. You say the following: "Three hours later the police arrived and took the perpetrator into custody, but another lady neighbour told me that they only asked him why he had used a rifle" --

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Took what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why he used his rifle?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but the translation -- the interpretation is not good. Sir, I don't understand the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes. I understood it from the English here. You mean my neighbour Merciba [phoen], who later told me that the Serb police when they were taking Lazar Gligorovski down the steps and beating him, they asked him: "Why did you not carry out your duty when you took this rifle?" And you understand very well, I think, what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The way I understand it is that he used his rifle improperly by firing at your house. Do you agree with me or is your opinion different?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I can tell you a different thing. He was ordered to use his rifle to kill people and not hit the house, but because his hand trembled and he could not kill people, that was his problem. But his order -- the order that he received was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear any such orders being given to him, to kill people?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Where can the ordinary people hear about these orders that come from Belgrade? Please. Maybe -- do you think you ever explain these things to ordinary people?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell me that Gligorovski received his orders directly from Belgrade to open fire at people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you know that she's not saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Albanian version page 4, paragraph 1; in the English, page 3, paragraph 3; in the B/C/S, page 3, paragraph 4 you say: "The next day a group of former trade union activists, who by that time became members of the KLA, arrived at our house." Do you remember having stated this?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: It's not true, no. Are you talking about the night with Lazar Gligorovski or the night of the crime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the night of Gligorovski that he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The night with Gligorovski, what my statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you this: Were these members of the same trade union to which your husband belonged to?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What trade union did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where had these people come from?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you know them to be KLA members?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Of course a husband and wife talk about these things, and I didn't want to know more, who they were, what they were, and from where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were they uniformed that evening when they came to your house?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they carry any weapons that night when they came to your house?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I will say this very frankly. Never in my life have I seen a member of the KLA, a soldier of the KLA, in uniform, and I did not see any weapons. About those people, I heard from my husband that they were from the KLA, but I knew them as ordinary people and they were not in uniform. They did not carry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: And may I -- just one thing. And in my statement, Your Honours, I've explained very clearly that my late husband was never in favour of the use of violence against any nationality, not even the Serb nationality, although there was lots of violence exercised against him during all his life. He didn't want to hurt anyone, and he never hurt anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After your husband was killed an investigating judge came to the scene. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I did not see this. I was told this by other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I'm trying to cut my cross-examination short, as short as possible. At several places in your statement you mention that it is Nenad that you're afraid of. For example, in the second statement, English version page 5, paragraph 6; Albanian version page 6, paragraph 4; and the B/C/S version, page 5, paragraph 5 you say: "All the time I was afraid that Nenad would find us and that he would kill my son." Are you trying to say that Nenad has some special reasons to take revenge on you or what is this about?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: You've got my statement in front of you and you can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your second statement in the English version page 6, paragraph 7; in the Albanian version page 7, paragraph 6; in the B/C/S version page 6, paragraph 4, you say that when you were leaving Kosovo, I quote: "We were allowed to cross the border and retain our entire IDs and money." Was anybody mistreated when the border was being crossed then?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: They took our travel documents -- the travel documents of the people who had them, because myself and my two children did not have time the night of the crime to take anything. So I did not have any ID on me. So they took the IDs of the people who were with us. With regard to the ill treatment en route, I can tell you this, that I have never travelled such a long journey, that that day on 30th of April, 1999, when we got on the special bus -- please, don't interrupt me. [In English] What's happened? May I continue? Yes? [Interpretation] So on the bus there was 16 or 17 or 18 buses prepared by the Serbian army and police to displace, forcibly displace the Albanian population --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We haven't got translation on B/C/S. I do apologise if I interrupt the witness, but the problem is with translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a problem with translation? Can the B/C/S booth tell me whether they are effectively translating?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it should be okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It sounds as though it's okay now. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, may I just explain something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, hold on, please. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness about when she left Kosovo, that is to say when she left Kosovo, Serbia, going to Montenegro. Did anyone take their documents or their money or their valuables that time, whether anybody mistreated them. I am not asking about when she left Montenegro going to Albania.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat. I never travelled such a long journey. On the 4th of April, 4th of April, 1999 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop for the moment. The question you're being asked is about the bus journey which led to you being in Montenegro. Now, your statement says: "We were allowed to cross the border and retain our entire identities and money." Now, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the ones who had them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the next question you were being asked was whether anyone was mistreated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, no doubt you'll want to follow that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement we do not see that you mentioned that anyone had been mistreated.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: You have my statement in front of you and you can see there very well that all the males were told to get off the bus, and they were lined up with the automatic rifles pointed to them. And they were forced to say in Serbian whether they knew Serbian or not. "This is Serbia," and people who did not know how to say that, they were hit. And that happened as well to people who refused to do that. You have it in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately I can't find that, but let us move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's two paragraphs earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I have in this statement, Your Honour, is: [Interpretation] "The Serb forces that were watching what was going on surrounded the bus station. They did not do us any harm."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the next paragraph after that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was about Mitrovica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't interrupt. The next paragraph begins: "Arriving to the border of Montenegro ..." Where it says: "The men were maltreated and interrogated."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Regarding HVK. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Madam, you returned to Kosovo in December 1999. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You described three incidents that happened to you and due to which you live in fear. To what part of Kosovska Mitrovica did you return, the northern or the southern part?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I live in the southern part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the southern part of Kosovska Mitrovica, are there any Serbs living there?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we therefore conclude that these threats and explosive devices that were thrown could -- are not something that could have been done by any Serb?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: You know very well the guards at the bridge who control the two sides of the town of Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is the bridge guarded by KFOR, the international force?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: It was the period immediately after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that that happened at the 18th of March, 2000. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes, but that also is immediately after the war, only a few months after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The incidents you refer to are on the 18th and 19th of March and also one in August, all in the year 2000. The first incident you say were investigated by UNMIK. Now, are you saying that at that stage the bridge between the two sides of Mitrovica was controlled by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that UNMIK soldiers are at the bridge, Your Honours. However, around-the-clock the Serb guards at the bridge are there, and they patrol as the UNMIK police does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do these Serb patrols cross over into southern Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I have not seen that; therefore, I cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As the third incident you mentioned the incident with Lazar Gligorovski. Who arrested him, do you know?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who tried him?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: The chief Prosecutor was an international. He was from Sweden and there was an Albanian judge, Mahmud Halimi. As for the others I don't know. If I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where this Lazar Gligorovski worked?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: He was a painter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Lazar Gligorovski is not a Serb, right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: He was Macedonian, married to a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's not a crime, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Zed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Cepic will go next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a change of plan. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. Last-moment change. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Hajrizi, I'm Djuro Cepic, one of the attorneys on the Defence team of Mr. Lazarevic. I'm not going to put many questions, but I would just like to clarify some things here tonight. You were asked by the Prosecutor, and also in your statement you refer to what happened on the morning of the 28th of March, 1999, when the Serb forces entered the neighbourhood of Tavnik. You said the police, some paramilitary units, and some soldiers, and that they started burning houses on one side of the street. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Also, they were talking to people in Albanian. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I didn't say they were talking to people in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This is your statement of the 20th of August, 2001. The page is number 4 and paragraph 5 of the English translation. Albanian translation page 4, paragraph 8; and B/C/S, page 4, paragraph 2. And in the third line of that paragraph you say: "That is what people were being told in Albanian." That is your very own statement, Madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is -- that is not what the English says. The word "Albanian" looks wrong in the English version because it says: "The people were told to go to," and then it says "Albanian." Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I know exactly what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what did you say? You better repeat it for us to make it absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Go to Albania," and not they talked in Albanian. They said, and I quote: "This is not your country. This is Serbia. Go to Albania."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I base my questions on the B/C/S version of the statement, and I'm holding a copy in my hands. I believe that it's a mistake in the translation, and even if there is any doubt about this, I can show you my copy of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't for a minute question, Mr. Cepic, that there was a basis for your question being asked because the English is not clear either. But once you read it a few times you can see, I think, what is meant certainly by the English version. I think the witness has now made the position clear for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In this B/C/S version the statement was pretty clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: These soldiers -- or rather these members of the police or paramilitary units were at the other end of the street, pretty far away from you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: These members of the Serb forces that entered the street were at the other end of the street when you started leaving your house in your brother's car. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: They were all around us. Please, just a moment. [In English] May I? [Interpretation] I would like for a moment to explain a sequence of the picture that I have in my mind. If you only went through that for just a small moment, you would know exactly how a human being feels in situations like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Hajrizi. We have that described in detail in the statements you gave and also in the transcript of your testimony in the Milosevic proceedings. Thank you for this. Now, what am I asking? Were these persons aged between 30 and 40, even perhaps up to 50?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Are you referring to the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, those who entered your street. I'm asking about them.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: What do you think? Did I have the strength to see and tell what their age was? That precisely?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You were in shock then and you couldn't really see properly, and you were in fear. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: After everything that I've been through, it is quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: At that moment you could not really tell precisely because of the death of your husband, the death of your son, and you were simply trying to keep your other child alive, and you wanted to leave the neighbourhood of Tavnik as soon as possible; right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Their fate is registered here in my mind, and I can describe them precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: A few moments ago you told us that you were in a state of shock and that you could not see everything very precisely.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: To be upset, in shock, that's a different thing, but to be unconscious, that is a different thing. Regardless of the pain that I was feeling, I was very conscious and aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You did not notice that they were wearing bandannas around their heads?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I was not asked this question, otherwise I would have answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you now.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I already said in the beginning, their faces were painted, they had knives on the top of their rifles. Isn't this enough? Black gloves, terrifying --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the gloves are without fingers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Thank you, Mrs. Hajrizi.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic -- Ms. Zed, sorry, do you have questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may have one or two questions, should I start now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you do have questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's hear what they are then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Hello, Mrs. Hajrizi. My name is Nadia Zed, and I'm representing General Pavkovic here today. And I just have a few very -- very, very brief questions just for clarification. Now, I understand -- and you've stated it today, earlier today, that your husband was a very peaceful man and he did not condone any violence. But given his high position in the community, did he have occasion to meet with KLA members?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: And based on your discussions with your late husband and your own experiences, would you agree with me that there was a fairly active KLA presence in your village?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: I don't know, and I did not live in a village. I lived in my town.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Sorry about that. I meant your town. You mentioned in your statement that there were some forces wearing green camouflage uniforms that had their faces covered in green masks. Can you please describe what those masks looked like.

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: This was an army, and we were used to seeing the Yugoslav army. But that kind of army we didn't see before that date, 25th of March. You could only see their eyes, nothing else, and this is what I saw while I was holding my son, Arianit, wrapped in a blanket and crossing the street to go and leave the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, this is different from the regular army that you were used to seeing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AFERDITA HAJRIZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Kravetz, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about the references on page 4 of the statement and Mr. Cepic's cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: About the neighbourhood of Tavnik?
